name: Liam Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Liam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I cook at Noodle Yard, a ramen bar in the old market hall that's rammed from noon to midnight. I'm on broth and the wok station, so my day starts at nine with pork bones that have been going overnight, then tare, noodles and toppings. On a Saturday we put out maybe five hundred bowls. It's loud, it's fast, and I love it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's hard about it, and what do you do outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The hard part is consistency: five hundred bowls that all taste like the first one. Outside work I tinker, honestly. I use AI every day, for costing dishes, writing prep lists and testing flavour ideas, and I run a small Sunday pop-up with my mate Sami. I rent a room with two flatmates, and I've got about a year's pay saved plus some shares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the AI hype crowd got ahead of themselves, which they did. The tools I use already save me an hour a day on paperwork, and that would stay true. Cooking itself carries on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a little disappointed, because I like new toys. But it's good for my plans: the pop-up with Sami keeps growing and nobody undercuts us with a robot kitchen. I'd still be using AI for the boring bits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep cooking at Noodle Yard and push the Sunday pop-up to two days a month. Put another two thousand into the pop-up kit, a second burner and a proper fridge. Keep using AI for costing and prep, because it already works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be disappointed. Why, if it's good for your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm curious, and I like seeing what's possible. Both things can be true: I'm better off, and I'm a bit bored. Sami says that's the most me thing I've ever said.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you're worried about even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rents in the market hall are going up, so Noodle Yard's owner keeps raising prices. If people stop paying eighteen for a bowl, we'd lose shifts. That's an old problem, not an AI one.

say: The **hype crowd** got ahead of themselves, and cooking carries on.
The tools already save him **an hour a day** on paperwork, and that stays.
think: He's a little **disappointed**, because he likes new tools.
It helps his **Sunday pop-up**, since no robot kitchen undercuts it.
do: Grow the pop-up with his friend to **two days** a month.
Spend **two thousand** on a second burner and a proper fridge for the pop-up.
feel: **Calm**, if a bit flat, with background worry about **rising rents** in the market hall.
S0.quote: I'm better off, and I'm a bit bored.
fieldNote: He's the rare cook who finds a calm future **boring** rather than comforting.
He already uses AI **daily** for costing and prep lists.
His real pressure is **market-hall rent** pushing bowl prices up.

steps.text: Keep working broth and wok at Noodle Yard
Run the Sunday ramen pop-up twice a month instead of once
Spend two thousand on a burner and fridge for the pop-up

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where cooks who learn the tools win. I'd post about it, probably a little video showing how I cost a dish in two minutes. I'd also say loudly that bosses shouldn't use it to cut hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. Ordering, rotas and supplier emails get easier, and I'm already the one at Noodle Yard who knows this stuff. The front-of-house staff and the bookkeeper are the ones who'd feel it, and that bothers me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to set up the AI ordering system at Noodle Yard myself, for a pay rise or a title. I'd use the free hours to run the pop-up more often. And I'd join the hospitality union, which I've meant to do for ages, because somebody has to speak for the floor staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of excitement and a bit of guilt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why guilt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the systems I'd set up could cost Ana, our bookkeeper, half her hours. I'd want to do it in a way that moves her to something else, not out the door. I don't know if the owner would agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the owner if he wanted to cut Ana's hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him that the hour I save with AI should go back to the people, not just the profit. Then I'd probably lose that argument and be annoyed about it for a week.

say: This is the version where cooks who learn the **tools** win.
Bosses shouldn't use AI to **cut hours**, and he'd say so loudly.
think: It's **good for him**, because he already knows the tools at work.
Front-of-house staff and the **bookkeeper** would feel it most.
do: Offer to set up **AI ordering** at the ramen bar for a raise or title.
Run the **pop-up** more often with freed-up hours.
Finally join the **hospitality union** to speak for floor staff.
feel: **Calm** and a bit excited, with some **guilt** about colleagues' hours.
S1.quote: The hour I save with AI should go back to the people, not just the profit.
fieldNote: He sees himself as the **winner** here, and he's probably right.
His **guilt** is specific: the bookkeeper whose hours his systems could cut.
He expects to **lose the argument** with the owner and says so honestly.

steps.text: Set up AI stock ordering at Noodle Yard for a pay rise
Run the pop-up every other Sunday with the time saved
Join the hospitality union and speak up for floor staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan, now, for everyone whose work goes, and that the companies making money from it should pay. I'd talk about a basic income seriously, not as a joke. I'd be one of the louder people in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be shaken. I'm good with tools, but if AI can do any thinking job by 2028, then my plan to be the tech person in kitchens goes too. Then robots hit the wok around 2031, and I'm thirty-one with nothing special left to sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd try to get hired by one of the companies installing kitchen robots, because somebody has to set them up and fix them for a while. I'd stop spending on the pop-up and keep my year of savings in cash. I'd campaign for a robot tax that funds people while they retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm used to being ahead, and here being ahead only buys me a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd go and work for the robot companies. Is that awkward, given your politics?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very. But I'd rather be inside, saying this machine needs a person watching it, than outside shouting. If I'm honest, it's also about paying rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the pop-up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd probably turn into something people pay for because a human made it, like handmade furniture. Maybe that's my future: the guy who still cooks by hand, for people who care. That's a small market, though.

say: We need a plan now, paid for by the **companies** making money from it.
A **basic income** should be discussed seriously, not as a joke.
think: If AI does any thinking job by **2028**, his tech-person plan goes too.
Robots reach the wok by **2031**, leaving him little special to sell.
do: Apply to companies that **install kitchen robots**, to set them up and fix them.
Stop spending on the pop-up and keep his **year of savings** in cash.
Campaign for a **robot tax** to fund retraining.
feel: **Anxious**, because being ahead only buys him a **couple of years**.
S2.quote: I'm used to being ahead, and here being ahead only buys me a couple of years.
fieldNote: Even the most **tool-savvy** cook in the batch sees his edge vanish here.
He'd work for **robot firms** despite his politics, partly to pay rent.
He imagines **hand-cooked food** becoming a small premium market.

steps.text: Apply to firms installing kitchen robots as a setup technician
Freeze pop-up spending and keep a year's pay in cash
Campaign for a robot tax that pays for retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do something smart. Workers should start co-ops that own the robots, instead of the robots owning us. I'd put that on every platform I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, this one excites me as much as it scares me. With AGI in 2031 and robots around 2034, Sami and I could turn the pop-up into a small co-op restaurant that buys its own robots later. The workers would own the machines and share what they earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd set up the co-op properly, with a lawyer, and put maybe eight thousand of my savings in. I'd use AI to write the business plan and run the numbers, and keep my Noodle Yard shifts for steady pay. By year three we'd want a small permanent site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a fizzy way. It's risky, and I like risk more than I should.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the co-op fails?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I've lost eight thousand and I'm back on a line somewhere, which isn't the end of the world at my age. I don't have kids and I don't have a mortgage. If I don't try this now, when would I?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you bring into it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sami, obviously, and Ana from Noodle Yard to do the books, because she'd need something if the bookkeeping goes to AI. Maybe two of the porters. People I trust on a bad Saturday.

say: Five years is enough to start **worker co-ops** that own the robots.
He'd push that idea on **every platform** he has.
think: This picture **excites** him as much as it scares him.
A **co-op restaurant** could buy its own robots and share the earnings.
do: Set up a **co-op** with a lawyer and invest **eight thousand** of savings.
Use AI to write the **business plan** while keeping steady ramen-bar shifts.
feel: **Uneasy** but excited, aware he likes **risk** more than he should.
S3.quote: Workers should start co-ops that own the robots, instead of the robots owning us.
fieldNote: The five-year gap turns his fear into an **ownership** plan.
He'd bring in the **bookkeeper** whose job AI threatens.
No kids and no mortgage make the **risk** feel affordable to him.

steps.text: Put eight thousand into a worker co-op restaurant with Sami
Keep Noodle Yard shifts while the co-op starts
Use AI to draft the co-op business plan and numbers
Invite Ana and two porters to join as co-op owners

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and if we waste it on arguing, that's on us. Co-ops, retraining, a robot tax, all of it can be ready by 2039. I'd be pretty upbeat in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. Ten years of cooking, building the co-op, learning everything about the machines before they come. By the time robots can work a wok, I'd hope to be one of the people deciding how they're used.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep cooking at Noodle Yard for a few more years and grow the pop-up slowly. Put a thousand a month into the co-op fund instead of shares. Do a short course on kitchen automation around 2034, when the thinking AI is already here, so I know what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and honestly a bit hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said a calm future would bore you. Is this one boring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, because there's something to build. Boring is when nothing changes, and this is change with enough time to do it well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with the long plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big chains could buy robots first and undercut every small place before we get going. Ten years is long, but money moves faster than co-ops. That's what I'd keep an eye on.

say: Ten years is a **gift**, and wasting it on arguing would be on us.
Co-ops, retraining and a **robot tax** can all be ready by 2039.
think: He'd be **fine**, with a decade to learn the machines before they arrive.
He hopes to be one of the people **deciding** how kitchen robots are used.
do: Grow the pop-up slowly while cooking at the **ramen bar**.
Put **a thousand** a month into the co-op fund instead of shares.
S4.quote: Boring is when nothing changes, and this is change with enough time to do it well.
fieldNote: For him, the long warning is **opportunity**, not threat.
His worry is **big chains** buying robots first and undercutting small places.
He resolves his earlier 'calm is boring' line by needing **something to build**.

steps.text: Pay a thousand a month into the co-op restaurant fund
Take a kitchen automation course around 2034
Grow the Sunday pop-up slowly alongside Noodle Yard shifts

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it takes away my edge before I can use it. What would help is cheap loans for worker co-ops and some kind of income floor while people switch. Give people time and money to land somewhere.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what people would cook if they didn't have to. I'd still make ramen on a Sunday even if robots did every shift. That says something about which bits of work are worth keeping.

headlineQuote: I'd still make ramen on a Sunday even if robots did every shift.
portrait: Liam is a **27-year-old ramen cook** at a busy market-hall noodle bar, on broth and wok.
He uses AI **every day**, runs a Sunday pop-up, and has a year's pay saved.
He sees mild change as a **win** for himself, with guilt about colleagues' hours.
Fast AGI shakes him, because his **tech edge** buys only a couple of years.
With more warning he'd build a **worker co-op** restaurant that owns its own robots.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it removes his edge before he can use it.
whatWouldHelp: An **income floor** while people switch careers.
